title: Security and Secure Development
blurb: Write secure code from the first line instead of patching it after a breach.

mustKnow.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 and how to use it effectively
mustKnow.body: The OWASP Top 10 is a list of ten web application risk categories ranked from real vulnerability data. In the 2025 edition, Broken Access Control stays at number one (now including SSRF), followed by Security Misconfiguration, Software Supply Chain Failures, Cryptographic Failures, and Injection. The new A10 category, Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, covers error handling that lets a system fail open. Use the list as a checklist when designing and reviewing code, but passing all ten items does not mean a system is secure.

mustKnow.title: Broken access control and IDOR
mustKnow.body: IDOR happens when the server accepts an object ID from the client and returns that object without checking that this user is allowed to access it. It is common because the code appears to work perfectly. Check authorization server-side on every request and deny by default. Hiding buttons in the UI or switching IDs to UUIDs only makes guessing harder; neither is an authorization check.

mustKnow.title: Injection and XSS: separating data from commands
mustKnow.body: Both share the same root cause: user input is spliced into a command (SQL, shell, or HTML). Prevent SQL injection with parameterized queries, and prevent XSS by encoding output for its context (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript) or by using a text API such as textContent. A common trap is that placeholders cannot stand in for column names or ASC/DESC; those need an allowlist. Even a framework that escapes output automatically can be vulnerable if you use innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

mustKnow.title: Authentication versus authorization
mustKnow.body: Authentication (authN) answers “Who are you?” (login, MFA, session). Authorization (authZ) answers “Are you allowed to perform this action on this resource?” A successful login does not grant access to everything: check both server-side on every request, and never trust a role or flag the client sends. In HTTP, return 401 when identity has not been verified and 403 when the user is known but lacks permission.

mustKnow.title: Password hashing: argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt
mustKnow.body: Store passwords as a deliberately slow hash with a per-user salt, so offline guessing after a database leak is very expensive. OWASP recommends argon2id first (at least 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1), then scrypt, and bcrypt for legacy systems (cost 10 or higher, and beware that it only reads the first 72 bytes of input). Never use MD5 or SHA-256 directly, even with a salt, and never use reversible encryption.

mustKnow.title: Secrets management and rotation
mustKnow.body: API keys, database passwords, and private keys must not live in code or Git. Read them from a secret manager (such as AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) or from an environment variable injected by the deployment system. When a secret leaks, always revoke and rotate it first and only then clean up Git history, because a copy may already have been cloned or scanned. Design for rotation without code changes, and enable secret scanning on the repo from the start.

mustKnow.title: Software supply chain: lockfile, SCA, typosquatting
mustKnow.body: Most of an app's code comes from dependencies, which OWASP Top 10:2025 ranks as the third-highest risk. Commit the lockfile and use npm ci in CI so every install gets the same versions and integrity hashes, including transitive dependencies. Scan for known vulnerabilities with SCA tools such as npm audit or Dependabot. Before adding a package, check the name carefully: typosquatting packages such as crossenv impersonate cross-env, and attackers may pre-register package names that AI tools suggest but that do not exist.
mustKnow.code:
npm ci                         # install from the lockfile only; fails if it disagrees with package.json
npm audit --audit-level=high   # fail when a vulnerability rated high or above is found

mustKnow.title: OAuth 2.0, OIDC and JWT validation
mustKnow.body: OAuth 2.0 lets an app call an API on the user's behalf through an access token; OIDC adds authentication with an ID token, which exists so the client knows who signed in, not for the API to accept in place of an access token. New apps should use Authorization Code with PKCE and drop the implicit flow, as RFC 9700 advises. When an API accepts a JWT, verify the signature with an algorithm you configure yourself (never trust the alg header, never accept none), then check exp, iss, and aud every time, and require exp to be present: some libraries, such as jsonwebtoken, skip the expiry check when the token has no exp.

mustKnow.title: CSRF, CORS and security headers
mustKnow.body: CSRF is another site tricking the browser into sending a request with the user's cookies. Defend with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, and never changing state via GET (SameSite=Lax still sends the cookie when the user clicks a link). CORS is not a CSRF defense; it relaxes the same-origin policy so other origins can read responses, so use an allowlist and never reflect every Origin value together with credentials. Add headers such as CSP, HSTS, and X-Content-Type-Options.
mustKnow.code:
Set-Cookie: sid=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

mustKnow.title: Least privilege and threat modeling
mustKnow.body: Give users, service accounts, database roles, and tokens only the permissions their job needs, so that a compromised component can do no more than its permissions allow. Threat modeling means working through, at design time, where data flows, what an attacker could do, and how you will prevent it. A popular aid is STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege), which helps reduce Insecure Design problems that are hard to patch in code afterwards.

mustKnow.title: Prompt injection in LLM apps
mustKnow.body: Prompt injection is number one in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: text from the user (direct) or from web pages, emails, files, and tool results (indirect) carries hidden instructions that the model follows. No defense stops it completely yet, so design for limited damage when it happens: give the agent the fewest tools and privileges possible (preventing Excessive Agency), have a human confirm important actions, and treat model output as untrusted data before rendering it, running commands, or calling APIs.

mustKnow.title: SAST, DAST and secret scanning in CI
mustKnow.body: SAST tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep scan source code for dangerous patterns, DAST tools such as ZAP test the running application, and secret scanning (such as gitleaks) catches keys that slipped into commits. Run them on every pull request and block only severe findings, so the team does not grow numb to alerts. These tools are poor at catching IDOR and business-logic flaws, so they cannot replace code review and authorization tests.

mustKnow.title: Input validation: allowlists and server-side checks
mustKnow.body: Input validation checks that incoming data has the format and values the system expects before it is used. OWASP recommends an allowlist (state what is allowed and reject the rest) over a denylist, which is easily bypassed, and checking both format (syntactic, such as a valid date) and business meaning (semantic, such as a start date not after the end date). Client-side checks help UX but can be skipped, so validate again on the server every time. A common trap is treating validation as a substitute for parameterized queries or output encoding; OWASP says it should not be the primary defense against injection and XSS (and a badly written regex risks ReDoS).

mustKnow.title: Session management: regenerate, timeout and logout
mustKnow.body: A session ID must be hard to guess; OWASP calls for at least 64 bits of entropy. Issue a new ID whenever the privilege level changes, especially after login, to prevent session fixation (the attacker sets an ID in advance and waits for the victim to log in with it). Use both an idle timeout and an absolute timeout, and make logout destroy the session on the server, not just delete the browser cookie. Set the cookie to Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite, and never pass session IDs in URLs, where they linger in history, logs, and the Referer header.

mustKnow.title: Cryptography: standard algorithms, GCM and a CSPRNG
mustKnow.body: Never design your own algorithm; use a proven library. OWASP recommends AES with a key of at least 128 bits (preferably 256) in an authenticated mode such as GCM, which gives both confidentiality and tamper detection, and says ECB should not be used outside very specific cases. Keys and tokens must come from a CSPRNG, not Math.random, which was never designed to be cryptographically secure. A GCM IV must never repeat under the same key (generate it with a CSPRNG or use a counter; one repeat breaks GCM's security immediately). Keep keys separate from the encrypted data, for example in a KMS or secret manager, so that a breach of either location alone does not allow decryption.

mustKnow.title: Error handling: fail closed and avoid leaking details (A10)
mustKnow.body: A10:2025, Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, covers systems that fail to cope with abnormal situations, leading to crashes, unexpected behavior, or vulnerabilities. Examples are showing database errors to users, which helps attackers map the system, and a transaction that fails midway without rollback (money debited but never credited). Catch errors where they occur and handle them, keep a global handler as the last safety net, answer the user with a generic message, and log the details server-side. When an operation fails, deny rather than let it through (fail open): OWASP says a transaction that stops midway must be rolled back entirely and restarted (fail closed), and denying access whenever authorization cannot be checked follows the same principle as CWE-636, Not Failing Securely (Failing Open), which this category covers.

mustKnow.title: MFA, brute force and credential stuffing
mustKnow.body: Brute force tries many passwords against one account. Credential stuffing tries username and password pairs leaked from other sites, and it works because people reuse passwords. OWASP considers MFA the best defense and cites Microsoft's analysis that it would stop 99.9% of account compromises; also block known leaked passwords, login throttling or lockout, and CAPTCHA. Login error messages must be identical in every case, such as “Incorrect email or password,” so nobody can tell which accounts exist. OWASP's password policy: at least 8 characters when MFA is on (15 without), support for at least 64 characters, and no composition rules.

mustKnow.title: SSRF: when the server fetches a user-supplied URL
mustKnow.body: SSRF makes the application send requests to the internal network or to the server itself. It arises in features that accept a URL from the user, such as webhooks, callbacks, or images loaded from an external URL (OWASP's example). The classic target is the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, which holds the machine's credentials. OWASP recommends an allowlist of permitted destinations, checking that the resolved IP is public (a domain can be pointed at an internal IP, as with DNS pinning or rebinding), disabling redirects in the HTTP client, and building requests only from validated data. A denylist of internal IPs is easily bypassed and is a last resort only.

mustKnow.title: File uploads: distrust the filename and Content-Type
mustKnow.body: An uploaded file is high-risk input. OWASP recommends allowlisting only the extensions the business actually needs, not trusting Content-Type because the client can set it to anything, and renaming the file to a random value (such as a UUID) to remove the risk of dangerous names (such as ../) and of overwriting existing files. Limit the size, store files outside the webroot or on separate storage, and allow uploads only from authenticated users with upload permission. For images, re-encoding the image helps remove unwanted embedded content.

mustKnow.title: Mass assignment: never bind the whole request to a model
mustKnow.body: Mass assignment (or autobinding) occurs when a framework automatically copies request parameters into an object, allowing users to set fields the developer never meant to expose, such as isAdmin=true or role=admin. OWASP lists these defenses: an allowlist of bindable fields, a DTO containing only editable fields, or a blocklist of protected fields. In practice, prefer the allowlist or DTO, because a blocklist must always name every dangerous field; a sensitive field added later and forgotten slips through (this conclusion is general reasoning, not a direct OWASP statement).

mustKnow.title: Security logging and alerting (A09)
mustKnow.body: A09:2025, Security Logging and Alerting Failures, covers systems that do not log important events, or log them without anyone noticing. OWASP recommends logging failed authentication, access-control failures, and input-validation failures with enough context to investigate, but never writing passwords, session IDs, access tokens, or keys to the log directly (OWASP says to remove, mask, or hash them first, for example replacing a session ID with its hash so the session's events can still be traced, while passwords are dropped entirely). Sanitize anything written to the log (CR, LF, delimiters) to prevent log injection, keep clocks synchronized across machines, protect logs from tampering, and set up alerts with response procedures, because a log nobody reads does not catch attacks.

mustKnow.title: CSP with nonce and hash instead of unsafe-inline
mustKnow.body: MDN says to avoid 'unsafe-inline' because it throws away much of CSP's value: inline scripts are one of the most common XSS vectors, and event handlers such as onerror are blocked by a normal CSP. The better option is a nonce, a value the server generates fresh for every response and places both in the header and in the nonce attribute of <script> (it must be unguessable and never reused), or a hash for static scripts. If a script carrying a nonce or hash needs to load further scripts, 'strict-dynamic' passes the trust along, but this protection is weakened if the script builds <script> elements from data an attacker can inject through XSS. Test with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only before enforcing.

mustKnow.title: Insecure deserialization and integrity (A08)
mustKnow.body: A08:2025, Software or Data Integrity Failures, covers systems that trust code or data without verifying its integrity: relying on libraries from untrusted CDNs or repositories, CI/CD and auto-update pipelines that skip integrity checks, or deserializing data the client can see and modify. OWASP recommends digital signatures or similar mechanisms and says not to accept unsigned serialized data from untrusted clients without an integrity check. From other sources: the Python docs state that pickle is unsafe because maliciously crafted data can run code during unpickling, recommend signing with hmac, and note that a format such as json may suit untrusted data better (values still need validation after parsing). MDN describes Subresource Integrity: add an integrity attribute (plus crossorigin for cross-origin files) as in <script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.min.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">, and the browser rejects a file whose hash does not match (a cross-origin file needs crossorigin, and the CDN must send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that permits the request, or the file is blocked even when the hash is correct).
mustKnow.code:
import base64, hmac, hashlib, json, pickle

# Risky: pickle can run code while loading; never use it on data the client can modify
prefs = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(cookie))

# Safer: verify the signature (hmac) first, then parse as JSON and validate
raw, _, sig = cookie.rpartition('.')
expected = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, raw.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
if not hmac.compare_digest(sig, expected):
    raise ValueError('tampered')
prefs = json.loads(base64.b64decode(raw))

mustKnow.title: Secure SDLC and NIST SSDF
mustKnow.body: Good security does not come from a single tool but from practices across the whole development lifecycle. NIST SP 800-218 (Secure Software Development Framework) groups its practices into four areas: Prepare the Organization (PO), Protect the Software (PS), Produce Well-Secured Software (PW), and Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV), covering people and process, protecting code from tampering, writing and testing secure code, and handling vulnerabilities after release. NIST describes SSDF as a starting point to adapt to each organization, not a fixed checklist, and as a common language between software buyers and suppliers.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user changes the number in the URL from /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 and sees another company's invoice. What is the correct fix?
options: Switch IDs to random UUIDs so that users cannot guess the numbers in a URL.
Filter the query by the user's owner_id and return 404 if not found.
Hide links to invoices that do not belong to the user from the web page.
Add a rate limit on this endpoint to prevent ID enumeration by any one user.
questions.explain: The root cause is that the server does not check permission per resource (IDOR), so putting the owner condition in the query fixes it at the source. A UUID or rate limit only makes guessing harder; the ID can still leak through logs, shared links, or other APIs.

questions.prompt: A report page lets users choose the sort column, and this code was reported as vulnerable to SQL injection. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Change it to ORDER BY $1 and pass [req.query.sort] as a parameter.
Escape the ' and ; characters in req.query.sort before concatenating.
Map the input key to an allowlist of permitted column names.
Configure the WAF to block requests containing the words SELECT or DROP.
questions.explain: Placeholders can only stand in for values, not column names or keywords such as ASC/DESC, so the query would not sort by the chosen column; use an allowlist instead. Manual escaping and a WAF can both be bypassed, because an ORDER BY payload needs neither quotes nor the blocked words.

questions.prompt: The comment system renders user text with this code. Someone posts and the code runs in every reader's browser. How should it be fixed?
options: Use div.textContent = comment.text to display it as plain text.
Strip the word <script> from comment.text before saving it to the database.
Set the session cookie to HttpOnly so scripts cannot read the cookie.
Enforce HTTPS across the site to prevent code being injected in transit.
questions.explain: textContent makes the browser treat the value as text rather than parsing it as HTML, which fixes the root cause. Filtering <script> is not enough because this payload has no script tag at all, and HttpOnly only limits the damage; the script still acts on the user's behalf.

questions.prompt: A legacy system stores passwords as unsalted SHA-256. The team proposes switching to SHA-256 with a random salt per user. Which statement evaluates this proposal correctly?
options: It is enough, because a salt makes precomputed rainbow tables useless.
Not enough: SHA-256 is too fast; use argon2id or bcrypt instead.
Switch to AES-256 instead so that passwords can be recovered for users.
Hashing twice with SHA-256 is already equivalent to password hashing.
questions.explain: A salt defeats rainbow tables and gives identical passwords different hashes, but GPUs can still try SHA-256 at an enormous rate per second; password hashing algorithms such as argon2id are deliberately slow and memory-intensive. AES is reversible, so a leaked key exposes every password.

questions.prompt: A developer pushes an .env file containing an AWS access key to a public GitHub repo and notices within 10 minutes. What should they do first?
options: git push --force to rewrite history so the commit disappears.
Make the repo private first, then plan how to fix it afterwards.
Delete the .env file in a new commit and add its name to .gitignore.
Revoke the key, issue a new one, and check the logs for its use.
questions.explain: Assume the key is already compromised: bots scan public repos constantly, and the repo may already have been cloned or forked. Deleting the file or rewriting history does not make the key safe. Revoke first, then clean up history and prevent a repeat.

questions.prompt: A project does not commit package-lock.json, and CI runs npm install every time. One day a transitive dependency publishes a new version containing token-stealing code, and it goes straight into the next build. Which measure prevents this most directly?
options: Pin exact versions (no ^) for the direct dependencies in package.json.
Switch CI to npm install --force so every install completes fully.
Commit the lockfile, run npm ci in CI, and scan with SCA before merging.
Load every library from a public CDN instead of bundling it with the app.
questions.explain: The lockfile pins the version and integrity hash of every package, including transitive dependencies, and npm ci installs exactly that. Pinning only direct dependencies still lets transitive ones float within the version ranges those packages declare.

questions.prompt: This middleware checks the access token an API receives. What is the most serious problem?
options: jwt.decode does not verify the signature, so anyone can forge a role.
exp is compared in the wrong unit, because a JWT stores exp in milliseconds.
The token should be moved into a cookie instead of the Authorization header.
The payload is still plain text and must be encrypted before it is secure.
questions.explain: A JWT payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone can craft a new one. Use jwt.verify with algorithms, issuer, and audience configured. exp in a JWT is already in seconds, so dividing Date.now() by 1000 is correct.

questions.prompt: An app uses a session cookie with SameSite=Lax and has a GET /account/delete endpoint. A signed-in user clicks a link on another forum and their account is deleted instantly. What is the root cause?
options: CORS is configured too broadly; the allowed origins must be narrowed.
The cookie lacks HttpOnly, so scripts on other sites can read it.
SameSite=Lax has no effect in modern browsers; it must be set to None.
Lax still sends cookies on link clicks, and deletion happens via GET.
questions.explain: SameSite=Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site POSTs and subresource requests but sends it when the user clicks a link that opens a page (top-level GET). State changes must use POST or DELETE together with a CSRF token. CORS is irrelevant: a link click is not a request that CORS controls.

questions.prompt: A company AI assistant summarizes web pages for users and has a tool that sends email on their behalf. The team worries that a page could hide instructions telling it to send confidential data outside the organization. Which measure best reduces the risk?
options: State in the system prompt that any instructions found on a web page must never be followed.
Limit the tool to in-organization recipients and require user confirmation before sending.
Filter out the phrase ignore previous instructions before passing content to the model.
Switch to a larger model so it can tell fake instructions apart much better than it does now.
questions.explain: No technique yet makes a model separate data from instructions reliably; system-prompt rules and word filters help a little but are easily bypassed. So limit what the agent can do (least privilege) and require a human to confirm actions that have real consequences.

questions.prompt: A reporting service connects to PostgreSQL as the user that owns every table. Later, SQL injection is found in a report endpoint. Which precaution, taken in advance, would have limited the damage most?
options: Use a longer, more complex database password than the current one.
Enable TLS on the connection between the service and the database.
Give the service a role with only SELECT on the report's tables.
Move the database into a private subnet unreachable from outside.
questions.explain: Once an attacker can run SQL through the app, they have the app's database privileges. A role with only SELECT on the required tables cannot delete, modify, or read other tables. A private subnet and TLS keep outsiders out, but the injection comes through the application itself.

questions.prompt: The signup form uses JavaScript to check that a username contains only a-z and 0-9 and is at most 20 characters, but the server writes whatever it receives straight to the database. Later, usernames with strange characters show up in the table. What is the fix?
options: Re-validate on the server with an allowlist; direct requests bypass the browser checks.
Obfuscate the JavaScript and tighten the client-side checks so invalid values cannot get in.
Switch the site to HTTPS so nobody can tamper with requests in transit and send strange values.
Add a server-side denylist of dangerous characters such as ' < >, which covers every case.
questions.explain: An attacker sends requests straight to the API with curl or a proxy, never touching the form, so the server must validate every time. HTTPS stops tampering in transit but not a user who sends bad values themselves, and a denylist is easier to bypass than an allowlist.

questions.prompt: The team says, “We already validate every field with strict regexes, so we don't need parameterized queries.” Which statement evaluates this claim correctly?
options: Correct: a strict enough regex removes all SQL injection risk with nothing else needed.
Incorrect: validation helps, but it is not the main defense; parameterized queries are still needed.
Correct: validating every field on both client and server means no other query style is needed.
Incorrect: a regex cannot check the format of user input at all, so validation does not reduce risk.
questions.explain: OWASP says input validation should not be the primary defense against SQL injection and XSS, even though it reduces exposure. Real names can contain characters such as ' (O'Brien), and a complex regex can miss cases, so separating data from commands with parameterized queries is still necessary.

questions.prompt: This login code has been reported as vulnerable to session fixation. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Shorten the session cookie's maxAge to just a few minutes so sessions expire as quickly as possible.
Enable HttpOnly on the session cookie so client-side scripts cannot read the ID.
Call req.session.regenerate() before storing userId to issue a new session ID right after login.
Rename the cookie from connect.sid to something far harder to guess so the cookie stays hidden.
questions.explain: Fixation means the attacker sets a session ID in advance and waits for the victim to log in with it; issuing a new ID after login makes the old one worthless. HttpOnly stops scripts reading the cookie but does not change the ID that was already planted.

questions.prompt: The logout button only calls res.clearCookie('sid'). The security team finds that anyone who previously obtained the session ID can still call the API after the user logs out. What is the fix?
options: Set SameSite=Strict on the session cookie so it is never sent cross-site, which closes this hole completely.
Clear the client-side cookie across every path and every subdomain of the site.
Switch to JWTs, which need no server-side session storage because they can be revoked instantly.
Destroy the session on the server (for example req.session.destroy) so the old ID no longer works.
questions.explain: Clearing the cookie affects only that browser; while the server still holds the session, anyone with the ID can use it until it expires. A stateless JWT is even harder to revoke before expiry, so it does not solve this.

questions.prompt: A site has an XSS bug that is not fixed yet, but the manager says, “Our session cookie is HttpOnly, so an attacker cannot do anything.” Which statement is correct?
options: Not necessarily: HttpOnly only blocks reading the cookie; injected script can still call fetch.
Correct: HttpOnly stops the browser attaching the cookie to requests made by scripts on the page.
Correct: HttpOnly blocks every inline script injected into the page, which prevents XSS entirely.
Incorrect: HttpOnly only works for cookies that are not also marked Secure, so it is rarely useful.
questions.explain: HttpOnly reduces the damage from cookie theft, but the cookie is still sent with requests started from JavaScript, so the attacker can act as the user without ever reading the cookie. The XSS must be fixed at the root.

questions.prompt: The function below generates tokens for password reset links. What is the problem, and what is the appropriate fix?
options: The token is too short; concatenate several Math.random results to lengthen it before emailing it to the user.
Math.random is not safe for security work; use crypto.randomBytes(32), which comes from a CSPRNG.
Mix in Date.now() so each token is unique and hard enough to guess for a reset link.
Convert the token to Base64 before emailing it so it is harder to guess than it is now.
questions.explain: Math.random is not designed to be cryptographically unpredictable, and concatenating outputs or mixing in the time does not change that. Base64 only re-encodes the data and adds no entropy. Generate the token with a CSPRNG such as crypto.randomBytes.

questions.prompt: A system encrypts card numbers with AES-256-GCM and stores the ciphertext in the customers table, with the key in an encryption_key column of the same table. If the database is dumped, which statement is correct?
options: It is safe: AES-256 cannot be decrypted without the key in practice, even if everything is dumped.
Base64-encode the key before storing it in the same column so it cannot be read directly from a dump.
The attacker gets ciphertext and key together and can decrypt; keep the key in a KMS or secret manager.
Use SHA-256 instead of encryption so no key needs storing and the card number can still be read back.
questions.explain: AES's strength means nothing when the key sits beside the data. OWASP recommends keeping keys separate from the encrypted data, so that access to only one place (for example through SQL injection) still does not allow decryption. Base64 is just an encoding, not key protection, and SHA-256 is an irreversible hash, unsuitable for data that must be read back.

questions.prompt: On staging (Express 5), testers see a full-page stack trace whenever the API crashes. The team wrote no error handler of its own, and NODE_ENV is not set. Which explanation and fix are correct?
options: Express always hides stack traces; testers must have enabled debug mode locally, so the code is not the issue.
Call app.disable('x-powered-by') and Express will automatically strip stack traces from every response.
You must set res.statusCode to 500 yourself before Express will hide the stack trace from the users.
The default handler sends the stack unless NODE_ENV is production; write your own and log server-side.
questions.explain: The Express docs state that an error with no handler of your own is written to the response with its stack trace unless NODE_ENV is production, and a trace containing an internal hostname is reconnaissance material for an attacker. Write an error handler that logs details on the server and returns a generic response; disabling x-powered-by only hides the framework name in a header.

questions.prompt: While the database is down, every user can open other people's documents. What is wrong with this middleware?
options: The catch only logs and falls through to next(), failing open when the check cannot run; deny or return 5xx.
logger.error marks the request as having passed the authorization check once the error is logged.
Compare ownerId with == because IDs from the two sources may have different types.
Move the error handling into the route handler, because this middleware cannot catch errors.
questions.explain: When getDoc throws, execution enters the catch and then reaches next() without ownerId ever being checked. OWASP A10 counts this fail-open behavior in the category; when a check cannot be performed, deny by default (fail closed). Switching to == is irrelevant and risks incorrect comparisons.

questions.prompt: A transfer runs as two separate steps: an UPDATE that debits the source account, then an UPDATE that credits the destination. One day the second step fails on a constraint violation; the code catches the error and tells the user only “An error occurred.” Which statement is correct?
options: No problem: the user is told about the error and can retry immediately without losing any money.
Money leaves the source but never arrives; wrap both steps in one transaction and roll back if either fails.
Retry the second step indefinitely until it succeeds, without rolling back the debit that already happened.
Disable the constraint that makes the second step fail so the credit always goes through, without touching other code.
questions.explain: OWASP A10 cites a transaction interrupted without rollback as a path to corrupt data or fraud. Telling the user does not undo the state that already changed. Wrap both updates in one transaction; unlimited retries or disabling the constraint create new problems and bypass the data's integrity rules.

questions.prompt: The pentest team reports that the login code below lets attackers discover which emails have accounts. What is the fix?
options: Change the 404 status to 200 but keep the email-not-found message exactly as it is.
Add a CAPTCHA to every login while keeping the two different messages as they are.
Return the same status and message in both cases, such as “Incorrect email or password.”
Lock the account on the very first wrong password so the attacker cannot keep trying.
questions.explain: A difference in message or status lets an attacker enumerate which emails exist (account enumeration). OWASP says to respond identically in every case and to watch for timing differences as well. A CAPTCHA reduces automated attempts, but the differing messages still leak.

questions.prompt: A system where every user must enable MFA has this password policy: “Must contain uppercase, lowercase, digits, and symbols, and be no longer than 16 characters.” Which change best matches OWASP guidance?
options: Keep the policy: forcing composition rules always makes passwords harder to guess, as OWASP recommends.
Lower the maximum to 12 characters to reduce the server's hashing load during login peaks.
Add a rule requiring at least two special characters so passwords are more complex and harder to guess.
Minimum 8 characters with MFA, support at least 64, drop composition rules, and block leaked passwords.
questions.explain: OWASP recommends a minimum of 8 characters when MFA is in place (15 without), supporting at least 64 characters so passphrases work, and no composition rules restricting character types. A short maximum length rules out secure password choices.

questions.prompt: A cloud-hosted app has the link preview feature below. The team worries that a user could submit http://169.254.169.254/. Which measure is most appropriate?
options: Checking that the URL starts with http:// or https:// is enough to block every internal destination.
Use an allowlist where possible, verify that the resolved IP is public, and disable redirects.
Denylist localhost and 127.0.0.1 in the submitted URL before fetching; that blocks every internal destination.
Set a 2-second fetch timeout to avoid lingering connections and prevent access to the metadata endpoint.
questions.explain: 169.254.169.254 is the cloud metadata endpoint that holds the machine's credentials. A name-based denylist is easily bypassed, for example with a domain that resolves to an internal IP or a redirect to one, so OWASP recommends an allowlist plus checking the IP after resolution. A timeout does not prevent access, and redirects should be disabled so they cannot bypass the URL check.

questions.prompt: A profile-picture upload endpoint checks only req.file.mimetype === 'image/png' and saves the file under the name the user sent, in public/uploads. What is the main problem, and what is the fix?
options: mimetype can be spoofed; allowlist extensions, use random names, and store files outside the webroot.
PNG is unsafe as a format on its own; accept only JPEG files instead, because JPEG cannot embed any code.
Files are not compressed before saving, so they waste server space, and that is the security problem.
Check mimetype again after saving the file to make sure it really is a PNG before the file is exposed to users.
questions.explain: The client sets Content-Type, so it is easy to fake, and checking it a second time is no better than the first. OWASP recommends generating a random filename and storing uploads outside the webroot. Choosing JPEG over PNG does not make a spoofed file any safer.

questions.prompt: A user sends PATCH /me with {"displayName":"A","role":"admin"} and their account becomes admin. Which fix addresses the cause most directly?
options: Hide the role field in the profile-edit form so users cannot see it or submit a value for it.
Change the endpoint from PATCH to PUT so users can only send the fields the server defines.
Check that req.body is well-formed JSON within the size limit before passing it to the update.
Pick only the allowed fields (such as displayName, bio) from req.body and pass those to update.
questions.explain: This is mass assignment; naming the bindable fields (allowlist or DTO) fixes the cause. Switching to PUT does not limit which fields get bound, hiding the field in the UI has no effect on someone sending the request directly, and removing only role is a blocklist that must name every dangerous field, so a sensitive field added later and forgotten slips through.

questions.prompt: The team added the log line below to investigate attacks on accounts. What should be changed?
options: Switch to logger.debug so this information is no longer stored in production at all.
Drop password from the log but keep recording failed logins with the user, time, and IP.
Stop logging failed logins entirely, because they contain users' personal data.
Base64-encode the password before logging; since it is no longer readable directly, it can be kept.
questions.explain: OWASP says to log failed authentication because it is an early signal of brute force or credential stuffing, but passwords must never be logged: remove them. Base64 decodes instantly and is no protection, and switching to debug or dropping the log entirely loses the data needed for detection.

questions.prompt: The company keeps failed-login logs for 90 days, but nobody looks at them. Then a customer reports their account was taken over, and a review finds thousands of failed logins per hour the previous week. What should be added first?
options: Extend log retention to one year so events can be traced much further back and nothing is missed.
Log in more detail by recording every request from every user as long-term evidence for audits.
Set alerts for unusual activity, with a responsible person and incident response procedures.
Move the logs to faster storage so they can be searched immediately after every event.
questions.explain: The data existed but nobody learned of it in time, which is exactly what A09 covers by including alerting. Longer retention or more detailed logs do not help without an alerting mechanism and people who must act on it.

questions.prompt: The team replaced 'unsafe-inline' with a nonce but hard-codes the value abc123 on every page. Which statement is correct?
options: Incorrect: a nonce must be fresh per response; a fixed one can be reused in injected scripts.
It is fine as long as the nonce is long enough and varied enough, even when reused on every page.
It is correct: using one nonce on every page improves caching and keeps the page just as secure.
Add a nonce attribute to every as well so the browser can load images under the policy.
questions.explain: A nonce works only because the attacker cannot guess the value used in that response; MDN requires it to be different and unguessable for every response. A fixed value is no better than none, and length does not help when the same value is reused.

questions.prompt: This endpoint reads user preferences from a cookie. What is the problem, and what is the right fix?
options: Set Secure and HttpOnly on the cookie so users cannot modify the values stored in their own cookie.
Base64 is not safe; switch to hex encoding instead of Base64 to prevent tampering with the data.
pickle.loads on client-supplied data can execute code; use JSON instead and sign it.
Limit the cookie to roughly 4 KB so that oversized data cannot be used to attack the server.
questions.explain: The Python docs say pickle is unsafe with untrusted data because maliciously crafted input can run code during unpickling, and recommend signing with hmac and using json; OWASP A08 likewise calls for checking the integrity of data passed through the client with a digital signature. Secure and HttpOnly do not stop a user editing their own cookie, and changing the encoding does not change the risk.

questions.prompt: A page loads the script below from a CDN. One day the CDN is compromised and lib.min.js is modified. What happens to visitors?
options: The browser runs the modified file and only prints a console warning, blocking nothing at all.
The browser automatically fetches the older lib.min.js from its cache to replace it when the hash does not match.
integrity only applies to files served from the same origin, so a CDN file is unaffected.
The hash mismatches, so the browser rejects the file and the script never runs, even if dependent features break.
questions.explain: SRI makes the browser compare the file's hash with the integrity attribute and reject a mismatch rather than merely warn (a cross-origin file needs crossorigin, already present here, and the CDN must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin). There is no fallback to an older file; features may break, but this is preferable to running tampered code.

exercises.title: Fix an API with SQL injection, an exposed secret, and excessive data exposure
exercises.prompt: This endpoint has three problems: it concatenates user input into SQL, hard-codes the database password, and uses SELECT *, so password_hash leaks into the response. Make it safe by using the pg library's $1 placeholder, reading the password from process.env.DB_PASSWORD, and returning only id, email, and name.
exercises.context:
Node.js + Express + pg (node-postgres)
users table: id, email, name, password_hash, created_at
The deployment system injects the database password through an environment variable named DB_PASSWORD
hints: Split it into three issues: user values in SQL, a secret in code, and more data returned than necessary.
pool.query takes (text, values): write WHERE email = $1 and pass the values as an array in the second argument.
Use password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD and change SELECT * to SELECT id, email, name.

checks.label: No password string literal in the code
Use the $1 placeholder in the SQL
Pass the user's value as an array parameter
Do not concatenate or interpolate user values into a string or template
Do not use SELECT * and do not select password_hash

exercises.title: An error handler that does not leak stack traces
exercises.prompt: This API's error handler sends the message and stack trace back to the client, revealing the system's internals to attackers. Change it to log the error details server-side with console.error, respond to the client with status 500 and a generic body that contains neither err.message nor err.stack, and, if the response headers have already been sent (res.headersSent), forward the error to the default handler with next(err).
exercises.context:
Node.js + Express 5
The error handler must take four parameters (err, req, res, next) and be registered after all routes
To keep it simple, this exercise returns 500 in every case
hints: Separate the details the development team needs (kept in server-side logs) from what the client should receive (a generic message).
Use console.error(err) to log, then respond with res.status(500).json({ error: ... }) without putting err.message or err.stack in the body.
Start the handler with if (res.headersSent) { return next(err); } so Express takes over once headers have already been sent.

checks.label: The error handler takes four parameters
Do not send err.message or err.stack in the response

exercises.title: Secure a GitHub Actions workflow for pull requests
exercises.tags: CI/CD security · least privilege · script injection · supply chain
exercises.prompt: This public repo runs a pull-request check workflow that accepts PRs from forks. Make it safe: change the trigger away from pull_request_target (it runs with the base repository's privileges, and this workflow also checks out and runs PR code, which GitHub documents as dangerous; newer actions/checkout versions block this case by default, so the original workflow enabled allow-unsafe-pr-checkout to skip that protection), restrict GITHUB_TOKEN to reading contents only, pin every action to a 40-character commit SHA instead of a tag, pass the PR title to the shell through an environment variable instead of interpolating ${{ }} into the script, and install dependencies with npm ci, which follows only the lockfile. The title must still be re-checked when someone edits the PR title (the edited event).
exercises.context:
GitHub Actions on a public repo
No secrets are needed for this task
actions/checkout v7.0.1 = 3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1
actions/setup-node v7.0.0 = 820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020
The PR title must start with feat or fix
exercises.starter:
name: pr-check
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, synchronize, edited]

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Check PR title
        run: |
          case "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" in
            feat*|fix*) ;;
            *) echo "PR title must start with feat or fix"; exit 1 ;;
          esac
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test
exercises.solution:
name: pr-check
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, edited]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Check PR title
        env:
          TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
        run: |
          case "$TITLE" in
            feat*|fix*) ;;
            *) echo "PR title must start with feat or fix"; exit 1 ;;
          esac
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
hints: There are five issues: an over-privileged trigger, a token with broad permissions, actions pinned to movable tags, user-controlled values interpolated into the script, and npm install.
Change on: to pull_request (keep the types that include edited so edited titles are re-checked), add permissions: contents: read at the workflow level, and change npm install to npm ci.
Write uses: owner/action@<40-character sha>, move ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} into the step's env: (for example TITLE), and reference it in the script as "$TITLE".

checks.label: Do not use the pull_request_target trigger
Restrict permissions to reading contents only
Pin actions/checkout to a 40-character commit SHA
No action pinned to a tag or branch
Pass the title through the step's env
Do not interpolate github.event directly into the script
Re-check the title when it is edited (types includes edited)

cheatsheet: Prevent IDOR with server-side authorization for each object on every request and deny by default; UUIDs are not authorization checks.
authN checks who you are; authZ checks permission. Return 401 for unverified identity and 403 for insufficient permission.
Prevent SQL injection with parameterized queries; prevent XSS with context-specific output encoding or textContent.
Hash passwords with argon2id: at least 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1, and a per-user salt.
When a secret leaks, revoke and rotate it before cleaning Git history: a copy may already have been cloned.
Validate input server-side with an allowlist for format and business meaning; validation does not replace parameterized queries or output encoding.
Issue a new session ID after login to prevent session fixation; logout must destroy the session server-side.
Verify JWT signatures with a configured algorithm, check exp, iss, aud, and require exp; never trust the alg header.
CORS does not prevent CSRF; use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens, and never change state via GET.
SAST scans source code; DAST tests the running app. Neither replaces code review and authorization tests.
